Sparrow (Doctrine)
SPAR-roh
n.
Old English spearwa; Hebrew tsippōr (small bird, especially the sparrow); Greek strouthion (sparrow). One of the smallest and most common birds of the ancient Near East, used by Christ as the supreme example of God’s particular providence over what the world counts trivial.

Biblical Definition

The sparrow is one of the smallest and most common birds of the ancient Near East, sold cheaply in the markets (two for a farthing, five for two farthings) as the food of the poor, and chosen by Christ as the supreme example of God’s particular providence over what the world counts trivial. The biblical sparrow-references are not numerous but are pastorally weighted. Psalm 84:3: yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts, my King, and my God. The sparrow finds her home and nests her young in the courts of the LORD’s house; the psalmist’s longing for the courts of the LORD is figured by the bird that has found her dwelling there. Psalm 102:7: I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top; the lonely sparrow on the rooftop becomes the image of solitude and affliction. But the supreme biblical use is in Christ’s providence-teaching: Matthew 10:29-31: are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows. Luke 12:6-7: are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God? But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows. The two parallel passages establish the doctrine. Several structural features mark it. First, the cheapness: sparrows were the cheapest of marketplace birds, sold at the lowest possible rate (two for a farthing in Matthew, five for two farthings in Luke—the slight discount on the bulk purchase emphasizes the cheapness). Christ’s choice of the cheapest bird is rhetorically strategic: if God’s notice extends to even the cheapest of creatures, His notice of His own children is incomparably greater. Second, the individual particularity: not one of them shall fall on the ground without your Father; not one of them is forgotten before God. The doctrine is not general providence in the abstract but particular providence over every individual sparrow. Third, the application by lesser-to-greater argument: the very hairs of the saint’s head are numbered; the saint is of more value than many sparrows; the Father who notices the falling sparrow notices the falling hair of His child’s head; the conclusion is fear not therefore. The argument’s pastoral force is the elimination of every reasonable ground for fear. If the Father’s providence extends to the smallest and cheapest of His creatures, His providence over His own beloved children is comprehensive, particular, and trustworthy. The sparrow-doctrine therefore organizes one of the most consoling pastoral teachings of the New Testament: the particular providence of the Father over every detail of the saint’s life, illustrated by His particular notice of the cheapest sparrows in the marketplace.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SPARROW as a small bird of the genus Passer; in scripture, the cheapest of marketplace birds chosen by Christ as the supreme example of God’s particular providence over what the world counts trivial: not one of them shall fall on the ground without your Father (Matt 10:29).

SPARROW, n. — A small bird of the genus Passer; one of the most common birds of the ancient Near East. In scripture, the bird of Christ’s great providence-teaching (Matt 10:29-31; Luke 12:6-7).

PROVIDENCE, n. — The act of providing or preparing for future use or application; foresight; in theology, the LORD’s comprehensive care over creation and His particular care over His people, illustrated by Christ in the sparrow-and-hairs-of-the-head teaching.

Key Scripture

Matthew 10:29-31 — "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows."

Luke 12:6-7 — "Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God? But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows."

Psalm 84:3 — "Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts, my King, and my God."

Psalm 102:7 — "I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top."

Modern Corruption

The sparrow-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the sentimentalization that has reduced Christ’s rigorous providence-teaching to a soft devotional refrain (His eye is on the sparrow) without the substantive lesser-to-greater argument and the explicit fear not therefore conclusion—and by the inverse loss of any sense of particular providence in much contemporary theological tradition that has reduced God’s providence to general oversight without the comprehensive-particular substance Christ’s sparrow-teaching insists upon.

expand to see more

The sentimentalization of the sparrow-doctrine has, in popular Christian usage and in much contemporary preaching, reduced Christ’s rigorous providence-teaching to a soft devotional refrain (His eye is on the sparrow, and I know He watches me, the spiritual’s famous rendering) without the substantive lesser-to-greater argument the teaching actually carries. Christ’s point is not chiefly comforting sentiment but pastoral argument with definite logical structure: (1) two sparrows are sold for a farthing (the cheapest of marketplace transactions); (2) not one of them falls without the Father’s notice (the particular providence over each individual sparrow); (3) the saint is of incomparably more value than many sparrows (the lesser-to-greater argument); (4) therefore fear not (the explicit pastoral conclusion). The argument is meant to eliminate fear at its roots, by demonstrating that the Father’s providence over each saint is comprehensive and particular. The recovery is the recovery of the rigorous argument: not soft sentiment but pastoral argument that produces fearlessness by showing the Father’s care to be incomparably greater than any threat the saint can face.

The opposite corruption is the loss of any sense of particular providence in much contemporary theological tradition. Process-theological and certain modern open-theism positions have reduced God’s providence to general oversight without the comprehensive-particular substance Christ’s sparrow-teaching insists upon. On these accounts, God does not know in detail every sparrow’s fall, every hair’s number, every detail of every saint’s life; He provides general direction and concern without the particular-providence the orthodox tradition has uniformly confessed. Christ’s teaching is more substantial. Not one of them is forgotten before God; the very hairs of your head are all numbered. The pastoral force depends on the particularity: if the Father’s notice were merely general, the lesser-to-greater argument would lose its weight. Because His notice is comprehensive and particular—every sparrow, every hair—the saint can be confident that his own life is held in the same comprehensive-particular providence. Recover both ends. Refuse the sentimentalization that loses the rigorous argument, and refuse the open-theism reduction that loses the particular-providence substance. The biblical sparrow-doctrine is Christ’s rigorous pastoral argument that produces fearlessness by demonstrating the Father’s comprehensive-particular providence over every detail of His children’s lives.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsippōr (small bird, sparrow) and Greek strouthion (sparrow); the cheapest of marketplace birds chosen by Christ as the supreme example of God’s comprehensive-particular providence (Matt 10:29-31; Luke 12:6-7); illustrating by lesser-to-greater argument that the Father who notices every sparrow notices every hair of His children’s heads, with the explicit pastoral conclusion: fear not therefore.

Hebrew tsippōr (H6833) — small bird, sparrow (over 40 OT uses; Ps 84:3; 102:7; 124:7).

Greek strouthion (G4765) — sparrow (4 NT uses; Matt 10:29, 31; Luke 12:6, 7).

Greek assarion (G787) — small Greek coin (the farthing for which two sparrows were sold; Matt 10:29).

Greek epilethō (G1950) — to forget (Luke 12:6, not one of them is forgotten before God).

Usage

"Not one of them shall fall on the ground without your Father—Christ’s particular-providence teaching using the cheapest marketplace bird as the rhetorically-strategic example."

"Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows—the explicit pastoral conclusion of the sparrow-doctrine: the Father’s comprehensive-particular providence eliminates every reasonable ground for fear."

"Sentimentalization reduces the rigorous argument to soft refrain; open-theism reduction loses the particular-providence substance; biblical sparrow-doctrine is Christ’s pastoral argument that produces fearlessness through the demonstration of comprehensive-particular care."
